effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative realist synthesis of secondary literature and policy documents; any numeric figures cited in the results (e.g., 408 remote/regional communities lacking safe drinking water, >500 remote communities with minimal water quality monitoring) are descriptive context drawn from included reports rather than a primary quantitative effect estimate.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Across 38 included sources, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander involvement in Australian drinking water policy is fragmented, inconsistent, and not legally mandated across national, state/territory, and local levels. National Australian Drinking Water Guidelines lack regulatory enforcement and the human right to safe drinking water is not enshrined in enforceable national, state, or local legislation, reinforcing urban versus rural/remote disparities (citing secondary findings that 408 remote and regional communities—40% Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander—lack safe drinking water and over 500 remote communities have minimal water quality monitoring). Overcoming entrenched drinking water inequities requires embedding Indigenous governance, self-determination, cultural knowledges, and long-term funding for transparent shared decision-making across macro, meso, and micro policy levels.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 8–10, Sections 3.1–3.9 and Figure 2; PDF pp. 10–11, Section 4

mechanism_certainty.comment: As a secondary realist review appraised with AMSTAR 2, the study is subject to a design ceiling of at most 2. Rated 1 because it synthesizes secondary policy documents, commentaries, and reviews documenting descriptive institutional gaps (fragmented multi-level governance, non-enforceable national guidelines, and unmandated Indigenous participation) alongside remote drinking water disparities, while explicitly noting in Section 5 that the authors could not locate local government reports or case studies comprehensively linking mechanisms and outcomes in drinking water policy.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 8–10, Sections 3.3–3.8; PDF p. 11, Section 5; PDF pp. 15–18, Appendix A

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines Indigenous participation/co-design and shared decision-making in water policy (participation), cultural tailoring and integration of Indigenous knowledge systems versus mainstream one-size-fits-all policy (accommodation), fragmented and misaligned responsibilities and complex bureaucratic navigation across national, state/territory, and local governments (institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination, BURDEN), and the absence of statutory human-rights obligations or regulatory enforcement of national drinking water standards (ENFORCEMENT).
